title: The Lucena position
summary: Reach the Lucena position and build the bridge that lets the pawn queen against the rook.
part.lucena.title: The Lucena position
part.lucena.summary: The winning position, why the king is stuck in front of the pawn, and the two moves that prepare its way out.
part.bridge.title: The bridge
part.bridge.summary: The king steps out and walks down next to the pawn, takes the checks and, on the fifth rank, the rook closes the bridge.
part.fourth.title: Bridge on the fourth
part.fourth.summary: With the black king close, a bridge on the fifth rank loses the rook. That is why it waits on the fourth.
part.rook4.title: Black rook on the fourth
part.rook4.summary: If the black rook takes the fourth rank, the king walks out without a bridge, because from so close the rook soon runs out of checks.
part.reach.title: Reaching Lucena
part.reach.summary: With the pawn on the fifth and the black king cut off, the pawn goes first, and your king climbs, check by check, to the queening square.
part.escort.title: King and pawn together
part.escort.summary: Before the rook cuts anything off, the pawn only advances protected by the king. When the black king comes close, the rook drives it away with check and cuts it off.
part.trade.title: Simplifying into Lucena
part.trade.summary: In 1999 Andersson trades pawns against Åkesson and simplifies into a Lucena, with the black king cut off.
part.rookPawn.title: The rook pawn
part.rookPawn.summary: With a rook pawn, the Lucena only wins with the white rook already on the fourth rank and White to move, so the king leaves the corner before the black rook gets organised.
part.rookPawnFar.title: Black king far away
part.rookPawnFar.summary: With a rook pawn and the black king cut off four files away, the rook goes in front of the pawn, faces the black rook on the b-file and opens the way out for the king.
part.zugzwang.title: Losing a tempo
part.zugzwang.summary: With no bridge possible, the rook loses a tempo without letting go of the black pawn and puts Black in zugzwang. Topalov beat Karpov this way in 2002.
part.summary.title: Recap and final test
part.summary.summary: The rules of the lesson on a Lucena from the other side of the board, and a whole Lucena for you to win on your own.
step.t_lucena: Pawn on the seventh, your king in front of it on the queening square, and the black king cut off by your rook. Before any explanation, count your king's moves. Which piece holds it on each side?
step.t_lucena.hint1: c7 and c8 belong to the black king; a7 and a8 to the black rook. Your king has no move at all.
step.t_lucena.hint2: Your rook can drive one of the two away. Which one, and with what move?
step.key: This is the Lucena position. Keep the picture: the pawn on the seventh, your king in front of it on the queening square; the black rook holds your king from the side, and your rook cuts the black king off by at least one file. This is a win, whoever is to move. {{Karsten Müller|karsten-muller}}, a German grandmaster and one of the great endgame experts, says it may be the most important position in all of endgame theory.
step.stuck: The problem is getting out from in front of the pawn. Right now the king has no move: c7 and c8 belong to the black king, a7 and a8 to the rook. That is why the first move is 1.Rd1+, which drives the black king away and opens c7. But opening the door is not enough: on c7 the checks come from the side and, with no shelter, the king goes back to b8. Watch.
step.stuckDemo: I will step out with the king without preparing anything, so you can see why it fails.
step.stuckDemo.m1: 1.Rd1+. The check drives the black king off the c-file, and c7 is free.
step.stuckDemo.m2: 1...Ke7. The black king stays close, two files from the pawn, ready to come back.
step.stuckDemo.m3: 2.Kc7, and the king has left the pawn's square. It looks like it is going to work.
step.stuckDemo.m4: 2...Rc2+. The rook checks from far away, and my king has no shelter anywhere on the c-file.
step.stuckDemo.m5: 3.Kb8, back again. Without shelter from the checks the king steps out and steps back: no progress. The bridge solves this.
step.push: Two preparatory moves. First, drive the black king one more file away, with check. Then lift the rook to the fourth rank: it is going to be the shelter.
step.push.hint: A rook check on the d-file pushes the king away; then the rook goes up to d4.
step.push.done: That's it. The black king is two files from the pawn and the rook waits on the fourth rank. Now your king can come out.
step.t_bridge: The rook waits on d4 and Black has made a waiting move. Now the king comes out. Which way does it go, and what does it do at each check?
step.t_bridge.hint1: The king never leaves the pawn: at each check, it comes down one rank beside it.
step.t_bridge.hint2: On the fifth rank the king stands just above the rook. Look at what the rook can do about the next check.
step.bridgeIdea: The idea of the bridge: the king walks down the c- and b-files, always right next to the pawn. Each check costs Black a move and the king comes down one rank. When it reaches the fifth, the rook that was waiting on d4 steps in on b4 and blocks the check. {{Nimzowitsch|aron-nimzowitsch}} called this building a bridge, in My System, 1925: the rook is the bridge under which the king crosses.
step.bridgeDemo: Watch the bridge move by move.
step.bridgeDemo.m1: 1.Kc7, through the door that 1.Rd1+ opened: a7 and a8 belong to the black rook. Now the king starts walking down.
step.bridgeDemo.m2: 1...Rc1+. The check on the c-file; if the king goes back to b8, it repeats the story from before.
step.bridgeDemo.m3: 2.Kb6, right next to the pawn: the king protects it and comes down one rank.
step.bridgeDemo.m4: 2...Rb1+. Check on the b-file, which also eyes the pawn: if the king lets go of b7, the rook captures it.
step.bridgeDemo.m5: 3.Kc6. c6 or a6, it does not matter; what matters is coming down one more rank without leaving the pawn.
step.bridgeDemo.m6: 3...Rc1+. The rook keeps at it, but each check brings me closer to my own rook.
step.bridgeDemo.m7: 4.Kb5: the fifth rank, just above my rook. The bridge is about to close.
step.bridgeDemo.m8: 4...Rb1+. The last check: between the black rook and my king lies b4, and my rook gets there in one move.
step.bridgeDemo.m9: 5.Rb4! The bridge. If the rook takes on b4, the king recaptures and the pawn queens; if it does not take, the pawn queens anyway. Black has nothing.
step.bridge: Now it is you. Black waits. Step out with the king and walk down the c- and b-files, always next to the pawn, to the fifth rank. When the check comes on b1 with the king on b5, the rook steps in on b4.
step.bridge.hint: The king goes c7, b6, c6, b5, always next to the pawn. On the fifth rank, the rook blocks the check on b4.
step.bridge.done: The bridge. The black rook has no more checks, and nothing is left to hold the pawn.
step.finish: Now the whole Lucena, with the d-pawn. Drive the black king away, lift the rook, come out with the king and close the bridge. Take the pawn to a queen.
step.t_fourth: The same bridge, but the black king has come closer: it stands on e6. 1.Rd5 would close the bridge right now, one rank higher. Is it good?
step.t_fourth.hint1: Where is the black king in relation to d5? Count how many moves it needs to get there.
step.t_fourth.hint2: If your rook leaves the fourth rank, what does the black rook do with the pawn on b7?
step.whyFourth: Why the fourth rank, and not the fifth? Because the black king comes closer. From e6 it cannot reach d4, but it can reach d5. 1.Rd5 now would be a serious mistake. Watch what happens.
step.trapDemo: I played 1.Rd5. It is Black's move.
step.trapDemo.m1: 1...Rxb7. The black rook gives itself for the pawn, because it knows what comes next.
step.trapDemo.m2: 2.Kxb7. I capture the rook, but mine is on d5, right next to the black king.
step.trapDemo.m3: 2...Kxd5. The black king captures the rook. King against king: a draw. The rook on the fifth was within the king's reach; on the fourth it would not have been.
step.trapRight: So how do we solve it? First a check on the sixth rank, to drive the black king away from the rook; only then does the rook go to the fifth. The rest is the bridge you already know, one rank higher: king b6, and the rook closes on b5.
step.trap: Now you. Check on the sixth, rook to the fifth, and the bridge one rank higher.
step.trap.hint: First the check on d6, pushing the king to the seventh. Then 2.Rd5, king b6, and the rook blocks on b5.
step.trap.done: Well done. The bridge works on the fifth rank too, as long as the black king cannot reach the rook.
step.t_rook4: The Lucena position, with Black to move. Black is going to play 1...Ra4 and stop your rook from going up to d4. What changes in your plan?
step.t_rook4.hint1: A rook far from the king can check forever. A close one cannot: from the fourth rank, after two checks it is within the king's reach.
step.rook4: The black rook on the fourth rank: the defence that looks cleverest. Your bridge on the fourth no longer exists. No harm done: the black rook is too close, and the king walks out right now, with no bridge. The checks run out by themselves.
step.emms: {{Emms|john-emms}}' line. Watch the checks run out.
step.emms.m1: 1...Ra4. The black rook takes the fourth rank: 3.Rd4 is forbidden.
step.emms.m2: 2.Rd1+. The same first move: I drive the black king one more file away.
step.emms.m3: 2...Ke7. The black king stays close, as before.
step.emms.m4: 3.Kc7. The king walks out with no bridge at all.
step.emms.m5: 3...Rc4+. Check on the c-file, from the fourth rank.
step.emms.m6: 4.Kb6, next to the pawn. The only other square was back on b8, and I would be where I started.
step.emms.m7: 4...Rb4+. One more check, but the rook is already two ranks from my king, almost within its reach.
step.emms.m8: 5.Ka6, next to the pawn. The checks are over: the rook on b4 gives no check to a king on a6, and if it checks on a4 the king goes to b5 and attacks it.
step.rook4Why: The checks are over, but the black rook still watches the b-file: if I queen now, it takes on b8 and it is rook against rook. A draw. The file still has to be closed: the white rook goes to d5, takes the two checks that are left and steps in on b5, in front of the black rook. The bridge on the fifth, once again.
step.rook4move: Black has pulled the rook back to b2, to check from a distance. Now you close the b-file: rook to the fifth rank, the king answers the check next to the pawn, and the rook steps in on b5.
step.rook4move.hint: 6.Rd5 first. On the check from a2, 7.Kb6; on the check from b2, 8.Rb5.
step.rook4move.done: Closed. The black rook has no checks, the b-file is yours, and the pawn queens.
step.t_reach: Now from further away: the pawn is still on the fifth, your king beside it and the rook cuts the black king off along the f-file. Which comes first: the pawn or the king?
step.t_reach.hint1: If the king goes to f5 first, the black king steps into f7 and the pawn gets no further. Which move takes f7 away from the black king?
step.t_reach.hint2: After the pawn, the king climbs the g- and h-files, using the pawn as a shield against the checks.
step.reachIdea: Before the bridge comes the road to the Lucena. The rook never leaves the f-file: it is what cuts the black king off. The pawn goes to g6, so that f7 is no square for the black king. And the king climbs against the checks, one rank at a time, until it stands in front of the pawn on the queening square. Then the pawn goes to the seventh, and it is the Lucena.
step.reachDemo: A rook-ending training position. Watch the order.
step.reachDemo.m1: 1.g6! The pawn first: f7 is now attacked, and the black king cannot step into it.
step.reachDemo.m3: 2.Kh5. The king climbs the h-file, beside the pawn.
step.reachDemo.m4: 2...Rh2+. Check again, now on the h-file: the king cannot stay on the rook's file and goes back to the g-file.
step.reachDemo.m5: 3.Kg5. The king returns to the g-file, one rank higher. Each check costs me nothing: I climb.
step.reachDemo.m6: 3...Rg2+. The rook keeps at it, and the king has to leave the g-file. The right square is on the h-file, next to the pawn: on f4 or f5 the king would block my own rook, and the win would slip away.
step.reachDemo.m7: 4.Kh6. Sixth rank, beside the pawn, which is protected.
step.reachDemo.m8: 4...Rh2+. The last useful check: the king goes into g7, in front of the pawn, and on the g-file the rook can no longer check, because the pawn is in the way.
step.reachDemo.m9: 5.Kg7. The king in front of the pawn, on the seventh. From g7 it watches f7, f8 and g8.
step.reachDemo.m10: 5...Rg2. Out of checks, the black rook goes back to holding the pawn. What is left is to bring the king to g8 and the pawn to g7.
step.reachMove: Finish the road. The king goes to g8 via the h-file, and the pawn goes up to the seventh. Recognise the position when it appears.
step.reachMove.hint: 6.Kh7 first: from h7 the king still protects the pawn (from g8 it would not: 6...Rxg6+). On the check from h2, 7.Kg8; then 8.g7.
step.reachMove.done: The Lucena, on the kingside. The black rook holds from the side and your rook cuts the black king off. The rest you know: check, rook to the fourth, bridge.
step.t_escort: Still far from the Lucena: the pawn is on the fourth rank, your king in front of it, and your rook cuts nobody off. The black rook attacks the pawn from the side and the black king is coming to help. Only one move wins here. Which one?
step.t_escort.hint1: Protecting the pawn with the rook, or stepping the king back to guard it, leaves the pawn standing still: the black king reaches c5 and it is a draw.
step.t_escort.hint2: Your king already protects the square in front of the pawn. It is the pawn that moves, not the rook.
step.escortIdea: The rule of the road: the pawn advances when the king protects it, never guarded by the rook. 1.d5! is the only winning move. 1.Rh4? or 1.Ke5? leave the pawn standing still, and the black king reaches c5; 1.Rb7+? is too early: 1...Ka6 attacks the rook, and the check has cut nothing. After 1.d5 the black king will come up to the pawn, and that is when the rook comes in: a check on the c-file drives it away and, from c7, the rook keeps cutting. Watch.
step.escortDemo: The pawn advances, the black king comes close, the rook cuts. Watch the order.
step.escortDemo.m1: 1.d5! The pawn steps to the square the king protects. Nobody can capture it, and the black king is one step further from stopping it.
step.escortDemo.m2: 1...Kc5. The black king comes up to the pawn, ready to step in front of it. Time for the rook.
step.escortDemo.m3: 2.Rc7+! The check pushes the king off the c-file, and the rook stays on it: from c7 it cuts the black king off from the pawn while the pawn advances. 2.d6 would also win, but with the black king glued to the pawn.
step.escortDemo.m4: 2...Kb5. The king stays close, but on the wrong side of the c-file: it cannot cross it.
step.escortDemo.m5: 3.d6. The pawn advances again, always protected by the king. The black king, cut off, can only watch.
step.escortDemo.m6: 3...Ra6. The black rook attacks the pawn from the side, but the king defends it; the attack leads nowhere.
step.escortDemo.m7: 4.Rc8. The black king wants to come to b6 and attack the rook: the rook goes up to c8 first, from where it keeps cutting the c-file.
step.escortDemo.m8: 4...Kb6. The black king reaches b6, and the rook is already out of its reach.
step.escortDemo.m9: 5.Kd7. The king steps in front of the pawn. After 5...Ra7+ 6.Kd8, the pawn goes to the seventh, and it is the Lucena: the rest you already know.
step.escortMove: Now you. The pawn advances protected by the king; when the black king comes close, drive it away with a check on the c-file and leave the rook cutting; then the pawn advances again.
step.escortMove.hint: 1.d5 first: the pawn, protected by the king. On 1...Kc5, 2.Rc7+ cuts (2.d6 also wins, but here practise the cut); then 3.d6.
step.escortMove.done: That is it. The black king is on the wrong side of the c-file, and the pawn goes up with the king beside it. From here to the Lucena is the road you already know.
step.t_trade: {{Skellefteå|skelleftea}}, Sweden, 1999, in a knockout event: {{Ulf Andersson|ulf-andersson}}, a Swedish grandmaster famous for his endgame technique, against {{Ralf Åkesson|ralf-akesson}}. Two moves earlier Andersson had two pawns against one and traded on purpose, keeping a single pawn. Here, with Black to move, Åkesson resigned, even though his rook was free to give checks. Look at the white rook on e4, cutting off the black king, and the white king next to the f-pawn. What is White's plan against the checks?
step.t_trade.hint1: The black king is cut off along the e-file. The f-pawn always advances with the king beside it and, when the king stands in front of it on the seventh, it is the Lucena.
step.anderssonIntro: {{Andersson|ulf-andersson}} had two pawns, e and f, against one. Instead of keeping the material, he traded the e-pawn and kept a single one, but with the black king cut off by the rook on e4 and the f-pawn protected by the king. That is simplifying: trading pieces or pawns to land in a position you know is won. This is what knowing the Lucena is for. {{Åkesson|ralf-akesson}} resigned here; watch the continuation the commentators give.
step.anderssonRoad: Black checks; the king hides beside the pawn.
step.anderssonRoad.m1: 81...Rg1+. The black rook starts the checks on the g-file.
step.anderssonRoad.m2: 82.Kf7. The king in front of the pawn, and the black rook has no check on the f-file.
step.anderssonRoad.m3: 82...Rf1. The rook goes back to holding the pawn.
step.anderssonRoad.m4: 83.f6. The pawn advances, protected by the king.
step.anderssonRoad.m5: 83...Rf2. The black rook waits behind the pawn.
step.anderssonRoad.m6: 84.Kg7, beside the pawn, clearing the way to f7.
step.anderssonRoad.m7: 84...Rg2+. Check on the g-file. The answer is to step in front of the pawn: on f8, the pawn itself shields me from checks on the f-file.
step.anderssonRoad.m8: 85.Kf8. The king in front of the pawn, on the queening square.
step.anderssonRoad.m9: 85...Rf2. The black rook holds the pawn again.
step.anderssonRoad.m10: 86.f7. The pawn on the seventh, the king in front of it.
step.anderssonRoad.m11: 86...Rg2. Do you recognise it? King on the queening square, pawn on the seventh, the black rook holding from the side and your rook cutting the black king off along the e-file. It is the Lucena, with the f-pawn.
step.anderssonLucena: Now the bridge. Here it is on the kingside, and one move does both preparations at once: 87.Rd4+ drives the black king one more file away and already leaves the rook on the fourth rank. Then the king walks down via e7, f6, e6, f5, and the rook closes on f4.
step.anderssonBridge: Build {{Andersson|ulf-andersson}}'s bridge. Check on the fourth rank, the king walks down the e- and f-files, always next to the pawn, and the rook closes on f4.
step.anderssonBridge.hint: 87.Rd4+ drives the king away and lifts the rook. Then the king goes e7, f6, e6, f5, and the rook blocks on f4.
step.anderssonBridge.done: The bridge on the kingside. {{Andersson|ulf-andersson}} never had to play it: his opponent saw it coming.
step.t_rookPawn: A rook pawn, which the rule says does not win: in the corner the king has only one side to come out on. But here, with White to move, it wins; with Black to move, it is a draw. Why?
step.t_rookPawn.hint1: Your rook is already on the fourth rank. In one move it reaches a4, behind the pawn.
step.t_rookPawn.hint2: The king comes out now, before the black rook gets organised. If it were Black's move, 1...Rb1 would forbid b7 and it would be a draw.
step.rookPawnRule: The rule: with a rook pawn, the Lucena wins only if the white rook is already on the fourth rank, the black rook is not on the file next to the pawn, and White has the move. The king steps out to b7 at once; when the black rook leaves the a-file, your rook goes to a4, behind the pawn, and the a-file becomes yours. With any of the three missing, Black holds, unless the black king is cut off far away: that is the next chapter.
step.rookPawnDemo.m1: 1.Kb7. The king leaves the corner now. The black rook is still on a1 and does not control b7.
step.rookPawnDemo.m2: 1...Rb1+. Check on the b-file: the king only has a6 or the corner, a8, and going back to the corner would throw the win away.
step.rookPawnDemo.m3: 2.Ka6, next to the pawn. If the rook returns to a1 with check, the king goes to b6 and nothing has changed.
step.rookPawnDemo.m4: 2...Rc1. The black rook changes plan: it wants to reach c8 and watch the queening square.
step.rookPawnDemo.m5: 3.Ra4! The rook was already on the fourth rank: in one move it gets behind the pawn. The a-file is mine, and the pawn is protected.
step.rookPawnDemo.m6: 3...Rc8. The black rook watches a8: if the pawn queens now, it captures the queen, and my king on a6 blocks my rook's file.
step.rookPawnDemo.m7: 4.Kb6. The king steps out of the way, and the rook looks after the pawn.
step.rookPawnDemo.m8: 4...Rc6+. The last check. It takes the black rook off c8: for one move, nobody watches a8.
step.rookPawnDemo.m9: 5.Kb5. The king escapes and still protects the rook.
step.rookPawnDemo.m10: 5...Rc8. Back to watching a8, but with no checks.
step.rookPawnDemo.m11: 6.a8=Q. The black rook has to give itself for the queen, and it is rook against king. With Black to move in the starting position, none of this existed: 1...Rb1 forbade b7.
step.rookPawnMove: Now you finish it. The black rook has left the a-file to head for c8. Put your rook behind the pawn, get the king out of its way and, when the black rook leaves c8 to give check, get ready to queen.
step.rookPawnMove.hint: 3.Ra4 first, behind the pawn. Then 4.Kb6 steps out of the way; on the check from c6, 5.Kb5 protects the rook; when the black rook returns to c8, 6.a8=Q.
step.rookPawnMove.done: Queened. The black rook has to give itself up for the queen. All of this only because your rook was already on the fourth rank and you had the move.
step.t_rookPawnFar: A rook pawn again, and your rook is not on the fourth rank. But the black king is far away, on f7, four files from the pawn. Your king needs to leave the corner via b7, and the black rook watches that square. How can your rook open the way out?
step.t_rookPawnFar.hint1: The black rook controls the whole b-file, and nothing drives it off for free: your rook has to face it on that very file.
step.t_rookPawnFar.hint2: Straight to b1 does not work: the black rook captures, and your king is stalemated in the corner. The rook has to reach the b-file another way.
step.silman: The other chance with a rook pawn: the black king cut off far away, four files from the pawn. {{Jeremy Silman|jeremy-silman}}, an American international master, teaches this idea in his endgame course. The rook goes in front of the pawn, to b8, along the eighth rank: from there it attacks the black rook on the b-file itself, and, since trading would hand over the pawn, the black rook has to leave the file; then the king comes out via b7. It wins because the black king is too far away to help.
step.farDemo: The rook reaches b8 along the eighth rank, and the king comes out.
step.farDemo.m1: 1.Rh8. Up the h-file, which is free, to the eighth rank. 1.Rb1? Rxb1 would leave my king stalemated in the corner: a draw.
step.farDemo.m2: 1...Ke7. The black king comes closer, but it is coming from far away: it arrives too late.
step.farDemo.m3: 2.Rb8! Rook against rook on the b-file. Trading does not help Black: 2...Rxb8 3.Kxb8, and the pawn queens. The black rook has to leave the file, and b7 is free for my king.
step.farDemo.m4: 2...Ra2. The black rook switches to the a-file and attacks the pawn, which the king will protect as it comes out.
step.farDemo.m5: 3.Kb7. The king has left the corner and protects the pawn. Now the checks come, and the king has to escape them without leaving the pawn; that is left for the exercises.
step.rookPawnFar: Now on the other side. Bring the rook in front of the pawn along the eighth rank, face the black rook on the g-file and get the king out of the corner.
step.rookPawnFar.hint: 1.Ra8 first, to the eighth rank. On 1...Kd7, 2.Rg8 faces the black rook; it leaves the file, and 3.Kg7. 1.Rg1 straight away does not work: the black rook captures and your king has no move, stalemate.
step.rookPawnFar.done: The king came out via g7 and protects the pawn. The rook in front of the pawn opened the way out, and the black king, far away, did not arrive in time.
step.t_zugzwang: Pawn on the seventh and your king in front of it, but the black king is glued to d8 and Black still has the g-pawn, which your rook watches. No bridge in sight. If it were Black's move, any move would spoil something. How do you hand the move back?
step.t_zugzwang.hint1: Try Black's moves one by one: the rook, the king, the pawn. Which of them does not make something worse?
step.t_zugzwang.hint2: Your rook cannot let go of the g-pawn. Can it lose a tempo without leaving the g-file? Count: after the black king's reply, whose move is it?
step.zugzwangIdea: This is zugzwang: the obligation to move. With Black to move, any move spoils something: the rook cannot leave the a-file, the king cannot leave the pawn, and the g-pawn, if it advances, falls. White needs to hand the move back without letting go of the g-pawn. 1.Rg6? does not work: 1...Kd7, and now it is White who must move in the position where it wanted Black to move. 1.Rg5! works: the rook keeps watching g4, and after 1...Kd7, 2.Rg6 arrives with Black to move.
step.tempoDemo: The rook loses the tempo, and Black has to give way.
step.tempoDemo.m1: 1.Rg5! A waiting move: the rook stays on the g-file, watching the pawn, and the move passes to Black.
step.tempoDemo.m2: 1...Kd7. The black king stays next to the pawn; any other move would give something up at once.
step.tempoDemo.m3: 2.Rg6! The rook cuts along the sixth rank, and now it is Black to move. Zugzwang: the king cannot go to the c-file, the rook cannot leave the a-file, and the g-pawn, if it advances, falls.
step.tempoDemo.m4: 2...Kd8. The king goes back to d8, the only square that keeps it next to the pawn and on the d-file.
step.tempoDemo.m5: 3.Rd6+. Now the check along the d-file pushes the black king to the e-file, away from c7.
step.tempoDemo.m6: 3...Ke7. The black king attacks the rook, but it has already done its job.
step.tempoDemo.m7: 4.Kc7. The king has left the corner, protects the rook and leaves b8 free for the pawn. The rest is technique you already know.
step.tempoMove: Now you. Lose the tempo with the rook without letting go of the g-pawn, leave Black in zugzwang and, when the black king returns to d8, drive it away with check.
step.tempoMove.hint: 1.Rg5 first (1.Rg8+ also wins, but here practise the waiting move). On 1...Kd7, 2.Rg6; on 2...Kd8, 3.Rd6+.
step.tempoMove.done: That is it. You won with a move that did nothing except pass the move: with Black in zugzwang, your king gets out of the corner.
step.zugzwangWhy: {{Cannes|cannes}}, 2002: {{Veselin Topalov|veselin-topalov}}, who would become FIDE world champion three years later, against former world champion {{Anatoly Karpov|anatoly-karpov}}. It is the same idea, one file over, and here Black is to move and in zugzwang. Why does no Black move work? The rook has to stay on the a-file: if it leaves, 73.Ka7 and the king escapes. The king has to stay on d7 or d8: if it goes to the e-file, my king gains c7, and the checks along the seventh and eighth ranks follow it. And the h-pawn, if it advances, is captured; without it, the white rook goes up to the fourth rank and it is the usual Lucena.
step.tempoPlay: Finish like {{Topalov|veselin-topalov}}. Black has just played 72...Kd8, back into the zugzwang. Hand the move back once more, take the king out on whichever side opens, and bring the pawn to a queen.
step.t_summary: A Lucena on the other side of the board, with the g-pawn. Before the recap, build the whole plan on your own: the first move, where the rook goes, which way the king comes out and where the bridge closes.
step.t_summary.hint1: Remember the order: drive the black king away, lift the rook, and only then does the king come out.
step.t_summary.hint2: The black king on e7 is one file from the pawn. Your rook has a check that pushes it one more file away.
step.summaryPlan: The plan is the usual one, just on the other side. First 1.Rf7+, which pushes the black king to d8, two files from the pawn. Then 2.Rf4: the rook on the fourth rank, ready to serve as the bridge. Then the king comes out via f7 and f8, with the pawn beside it. Look at the black rook: it is on the short side, right next to the pawn, and its checks run out quickly; the bridge will not even be needed, but the rook is already in the right place if it is.
step.summaryMove: Do the preparation right here: drive the black king away with check and lift the rook to the fourth rank.
step.summaryMove.hint: 1.Rf7+ pushes the king to d8; then 2.Rf4, and the rook waits on the fourth.
step.summaryMove.done: Done: the black king driven away and the rook on the fourth rank. Now the king comes out along the f-file, and the rook, on the fourth, closes the bridge if the checks come.
step.recap: Four rules to take with you. One: king in front of the pawn on the queening square, enemy king cut off, is the Lucena. Two: to get there, the pawn advances protected by the king, the rook cuts the black king off, with check if it comes close, and it is worth trading material to land in it.
step.recap2: Three: check to drive the king away and rook to the fourth rank; the king walks down next to the pawn and the rook closes the bridge; the fifth only with the black king far away, and, if the black rook is too close, the king walks out with no bridge. Four: with a rook pawn, it only wins with the rook already on the fourth and the move, or with the black king cut off four files away. And remember: not every position that looks like this wins. If the black king is not cut off and the black rook checks from far away, from the side, it is the short-side lesson's defence.
step.lastPlay: The last Lucena of the lesson, and this one is all yours: the black king is far away, on g7. Decide for yourself whether the bridge closes on the fourth or the fifth rank, and take the pawn to a queen.
ex.e12: A king's pawn, and the black rook reached the fourth rank first: there is no bridge there. How does White make progress? Find the winning move.
ex.e12.hint: First drive the black king away with a check. Then ask whether your king really needs shelter: the black rook is too close to keep checking for long.
ex.e12.solution: 1.Rc1+ drives the king to b7, and 2.Kd7! walks out at once, with no bridge. The checks soon run out: 2...Rd4+ 3.Ke6, 3...Re4+ 4.Kd6, and the white rook comes back along the d-file (5.Rd1, 6.Rd5+) to shut the road on the fifth rank. Other moves also win, but walking out with the king is the shortest road: with the black rook so close, the king needs no bridge. Hawkins' line.
ex.e13: Andersson vs Åkesson, Skellefteå, 1999. Two pawns against one, but the clearest road goes through a position you already know. Find the winning move.
ex.e13.hint: With a single pawn, which position do you want on the board? Look for a pawn trade that leaves the black king cut off.
ex.e13.solution: 79.e4! After 79...dxe4 80.Rxe4, the black king is cut off by the rook and the f-pawn, with the white king beside it, goes on to the Lucena. The game went 80...Kd7 81.Kg6 and Black resigned. 79.Re6+, 79.Re7 and 79.Re8 also win, but 79.e4 is Andersson's idea: trade into the position you know is won.
ex.e14: The pawn is still on the third rank and the black rook is already attacking it. Take the pawn forward without letting the black king come back. Find the winning move.
ex.e14.hint: The pawn advances protected by the king, not by the rook. When the black king comes close, the rook cuts it off along the file.
ex.e14.solution: 1.e4! The king on f5 protects the pawn (1.Rb7+ also wins). After 1...Kc5, 2.e5 moves on again, and when the black king reaches d5, 3.Rd7+ cuts it off along the d-file. From there it is the known road: pawn on the seventh, king in front, bridge. Defending the pawn with the rook or moving the king away from f5 draws.
ex.e15: A rook's pawn, which nearly always draws. Here there is a chance, and only because White has the move. Find it.
ex.e15.hint: The black king sits next to the b-file and locks your king in the corner. Push it away first; the rook on the fourth rank does the rest.
ex.e15.solution: 1.Rc4+! drives the black king to d7. Then 2.Kb7 leaves the corner, and after the check on b1 the king goes to a6, next to the pawn: with the rook already on the fourth rank, the checks run out and the pawn promotes. With Black to move, 1...Rc1 or 1...Kc7 holds the draw. With a rook's pawn, the Lucena only wins in two cases: this one, with the rook already on the fourth rank and White to move, or with the black king cut off far away.
ex.e16: Topalov vs Karpov, Cannes, 2002. The black king is right next to the pawn and Black still has the h-pawn. No bridge in sight. What now? Find the winning move.
ex.e16.hint: Your rook cannot let go of the h-pawn. Look for the position where Black, having to move, must give something up.
ex.e16.solution: Topalov played 70.Rh7+ Kd8 71.Rh8+ Kd7 72.Rh6! The starting position again, now with Black to move. It is zugzwang: every Black move makes things worse. The h-pawn falls, the king steps away from the pawn, or the rook leaves the a-file and the white king gets out. The game went 72...Kd8 73.Rh7 Rb4 74.Ka7 Ra4+ 75.Kb6 and Karpov resigned. The rook loses a tempo without leaving the h-file: 70.Rh8 on the first move, or 71.Rh6 and 71.Rh5 on the second, also win.
ex.e17: A rook's pawn again, but now the black king is far away. This is Silman's line, after 1.Rc1 Ke7. Every move counts, right to the end. Find the winning move.
ex.e17.hint: The rook goes in front of the pawn, along the b-file, so the king can get out. Then the king walks towards the black king, and at the end there is a sacrifice.
ex.e17.solution: 2.Rc8 and 3.Rb8: the rook on the b-file frees the king. 3...Ra2, and 4.Kb7 steps out; the king escapes the checks via c8 and d8, towards the black king. When the black rook goes to h2, 7.Rb6+ Kc5 and 8.Rc6+! If 8...Kxc6, 9.a8=Q+ and it is queen against rook, which wins; if the king runs, the rook goes back and the pawn promotes. With a rook's pawn, the Lucena only wins in two cases: this one, with the black king cut off far away, or with the rook already on the fourth rank and White to move.
key.lucena: The Lucena position as Alessandro Salvio published it in 1634: the pawn is one step from promoting and the white king stands in front of it. White wins whoever moves: all that is left is to build the bridge.
key.villa5: Another Lucena, with the black king further away. The rook can build the bridge on the fourth rank, the safest way, but the fifth works too.
key.rook4: The Lucena position with Black to move: the black rook goes to the fourth rank and stops the bridge there. White still wins by building it one rank higher.
key.shortSide: The exception: Black is to move, and the black rook, far from the pawn, checks from the side without end. A draw. This is the short-side lesson's defence.
key.practiceBridge: The Lucena on the other side of the board: the rook gives one check to push the black king away, goes to the fourth rank and from there becomes the bridge.
key.escort: The road to the Lucena: the pawn only advances when the king protects it, and the rook, which cuts nothing yet, waits for the black king to come close so it can drive it away with check and keep cutting.
key.andersson: Andersson vs Åkesson, 1999: Black resigned here. The white king is beside the pawn, and nothing can stop the Lucena position from appearing.
key.rookPawn: With a rook pawn the Lucena does not always win. Here everything depends on the move: with White to play, the king gets out of the corner in time and wins; with Black to play, the rook traps the king and draws.
key.zugzwang: Zugzwang with the pawn on the seventh: with Black to move, any move gives something up. With no bridge in sight, the rook loses a tempo without letting go of the black pawn and hands the move back. That is how Topalov beat Karpov in 2002.
history: The Lucena position is the most important one in rook endings: with rook and pawn against rook it is the position that wins, and almost every ending of this kind revolves around reaching it or preventing it. The name is a historical mistake: the Spaniard Luis Ramírez de Lucena wrote one of the first printed chess books around 1497, but the position is not in it; it first appears in 1634, in a book by the Italian Alessandro Salvio. The idea of "building a bridge" with the rook, which is the heart of this lesson, got its name from Aron Nimzowitsch in 1925. Grandmasters know it so well that they rarely need to play it out: in 1999, in Sweden, Ulf Andersson exchanged pawns just to reach it, and his opponent resigned before the bridge ever appeared on the board. In 2002, in Cannes, Veselin Topalov beat Anatoly Karpov in a similar position where no bridge was possible, with a trick to hand over the move.
practice: Now the real ending: rook and pawn against rook, with your king far away and the black rook active. Bring the king in front of the pawn, cut the black king off and look for the Lucena. I will be checking the bridge.
